Clinical Vignette: Margaret

Margaret is a seventy-one-year-old woman who spent forty-three years working as a forensic analyst for the state crime laboratory. She had built a reputation as meticulous and unflappable—the kind of professional who could spend eight hours examining trace evidence under a microscope without losing focus. Her colleagues respected her; defendants' attorneys knew her testimony would be thorough and credible. She had seen photographs of terrible things, had handled evidence from violent crimes, had sat in courtrooms describing what she found. She thought she understood violence in an intellectual way.

Three years ago, Margaret was assaulted in the parking garage of her laboratory building at 6:15 in the evening. A man she had never seen before grabbed her from behind as she walked to her car, struck her repeatedly, and attempted to take her purse. A security guard heard her screaming and intervened. The man fled. Margaret sustained a fractured rib, significant bruising, and lacerations on her face and arms. The physical injuries healed within weeks.

What did not heal was something else entirely.

For the first months after the assault, Margaret experienced what she describes as "living in a fog." She would start tasks and forget why she had begun them. She retired from her position—a decision she made almost automatically, without deliberation. Her husband, Robert, noticed that she had stopped going to their book club, had stopped tending to the garden she had maintained for thirty years. When he asked if she wanted to go out for dinner, she would agree, then become anxious in the car and ask to return home.

Now, three years later, Margaret sits in her living room most days. The assault happened in a parking garage, and she has not driven at night since. She no longer drives at all, actually—the thought of being in an enclosed space, unable to escape, sends her heart racing. Robert drives her to her medical appointments. She has not been inside a grocery store in eighteen months; she orders everything online. When Robert suggests they visit their daughter two states away, Margaret's chest tightens and she cannot articulate why, only that she cannot do it.

What troubles Margaret most is the way her mind now works. She will be sitting in her living room, reading, and suddenly she is in the parking garage again—not remembering it, but there, feeling the hands on her shoulders, the impact of the blows. These episodes last anywhere from seconds to several minutes. When they end, she feels exhausted and disoriented. She has stopped reading in the afternoons because the episodes come more frequently then, and she cannot explain this pattern to herself.

She startles at sounds. The mailman's knock at the door sends adrenaline through her body. Robert has learned not to approach her from behind. She sleeps poorly, waking at 3 a.m. with her heart pounding, sometimes unsure for several minutes where she is. She has gained weight—she eats when anxious, which is almost constantly—and she knows this troubles Robert, though he does not say so.

Margaret finds it difficult to reconcile this version of herself with the woman she was. The woman who examined evidence from assaults, who understood violence academically, who had testified about brutal crimes. She wonders if that woman was naive, if she never truly grasped what violence was until it happened to her. She wonders if she will ever feel safe again, or if this—this constant vigilance, this imprisonment in her own home—is simply what her life is now.
